investigations.title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
investigations.title_es: Experimento de fuego de naves espaciales-II
investigations.objective: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
investigations.approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
investigations.research_impacts: The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

Two cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, pressure and CO2/O2 sensors, and anemometers recorded large-scale flame growth and the thermal environment throughout the burn.

El experimento estableció una plataforma realista de incendio en microgravedad para comparar los límites de inflamabilidad en baja gravedad con el ensayo de cribado de la NASA en gravedad normal.

limitations_es: El ensayo utilizó un solo material y una sola velocidad de flujo en una nave de carga no tripulada, por lo que persisten las incógnitas sobre geometría y ventilación específicas de un hábitat.

investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.title_es: Quema y Supresión de Sólidos
investigations.objective:
The two main objectives for BASS are to:
 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
investigations.approach:
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
investigations.research_impacts:
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

investigations.summary_es:
Los dos objetivos principales de BASS son:
 1.) Comenzar a cerrar la brecha entre el método de prueba #1 de gravedad normal NASA-STD-6001, las pruebas de microgravedad terrestres y la inflamabilidad real del material en microgravedad. La relación entre estos puede investigarse observando las llamas ardiendo durante los tiempos más largos disponibles en vuelo. La selección actual de materiales de las naves espaciales de la NASA se basa en un método de prueba estándar (NASA–STD–6001 Prueba 1) que segrega el material según el comportamiento de 1 g sin considerar los efectos de la baja gravedad.
key_findings: BASS burned cotton/fiberglass fabric, Nomex, and Ultem samples in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox at airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s, in concurrent and opposed flow.
It assessed the effectiveness of an inert gaseous extinguishing agent similar to the ISS system, and measured flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and quenching behavior.
The results provide radiative heat-emission data for first-order spacecraft fire models and support performance-based material selection beyond NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
key_findings_es: BASS quemó muestras de tela de algodón/fibra de vidrio, Nomex y Ultem en la guantera de microgravedad de la ISS con velocidades de aire de hasta 40 cm/s, en flujo concurrente y opuesto.
Evaluó la eficacia de un agente extintor gaseoso inerte similar al del sistema de la ISS y midió tamaño, forma, color, velocidad de propagación y extinción de la llama.

Los resultados aportan datos de emisión de calor por radiación para modelos de primer orden de incendios en naves y respaldan una selección de materiales basada en desempeño más allá del ensayo NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
limitations: The sample set and flow duct are small compared with a spacecraft compartment, and only one extinguishing-agent concept was evaluated.
The public record does not report the measured spread rates or agent concentrations; those remain in the mission data and publications.
limitations_es: El conjunto de muestras y el conducto de flujo son pequeños en comparación con un compartimento de nave, y solo se evaluó un concepto de agente extintor.
El registro público no reporta las velocidades de propagación ni las concentraciones de agente medidas; estos datos permanecen en la misión y en las publicaciones.

investigations.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
investigations.title_es: Quema y Supresión de Sólidos - II
investigations.objective:
BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements.
 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.

The primary variables include:
 • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction)
 • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation)
 • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets
investigations.approach: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.
investigations.research_impacts: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

investigations.summary_en:
BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include:
 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it.
investigations.summary_es:
Los resultados de BASS-II contribuyen a los modelos computacionales de combustión utilizados en el diseño de sistemas de detección y extinción de incendios en microgravedad y en la Tierra. Los objetivos incluyen:
 1) Estudiar los límites de ignición, crecimiento de llama, propagación de llama y extinción de combustibles sólidos que queman en flujos forzados de baja velocidad en microgravedad. Un objetivo principal de BASS-II es mejorar la seguridad contra incendios de las naves espaciales, mejorar la comprensión de la combustión en el espacio y cómo evitarla.
key_findings: BASS-II burned thick solid fuels—slabs, cylinders, spherical sections, films, and fabrics—in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox under forced flows up to 40 cm/s and oxygen concentrations below 21%.
It measured ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction in opposed and concurrent flow, and related these to material geometry and ambient oxygen.
The campaign was designed to bridge NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual microgravity flammability, and to provide preliminary data for SoFIE.
key_findings_es: BASS-II quemó combustibles sólidos gruesos —placas, cilindros, secciones esféricas, películas y telas— en la guantera de microgravedad de la ISS con flujos forzados de hasta 40 cm/s y concentraciones de oxígeno inferiores al 21%.
Midió ignición, crecimiento de llama, propagación y extinción en flujo opuesto y concurrente, y las relacionó con la geometría del material y el oxígeno ambiente.

La campaña se diseñó para tender un puente entre el ensayo NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, los ensayos de microgravedad en tierra y la inflamabilidad real en microgravedad, y para aportar datos preliminares a SoFIE.
limitations: The glovebox wind tunnel limits sample size and flow range, and the tests only reduced oxygen below 21%, leaving enriched-oxygen environments uncharacterized.
Public metadata does not include the tabulated flammability limits; quantitative use requires the BASS-II data products and publications.
limitations_es: El túnel de viento de la guantera limita el tamaño de muestra y el rango de flujo, y los ensayos solo redujeron el oxígeno por debajo del 21%, dejando sin caracterizar atmósferas enriquecidas.
Los metadatos públicos no incluyen las tablas de límites de inflamabilidad; su uso cuantitativo requiere los productos de datos y las publicaciones de BASS-II.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.title_es: Experimento de extinción de llamas
investigations.objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
investigations.approach:
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
 4. Perform a droplet combustion test.
 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
 6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.

There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow. In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).

The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.
investigations.research_impacts: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

investigations.summary_es: La investigación FLEX (Experimento de extinción de llamas) tiene como objetivo mapear los límites de inflamabilidad de los combustibles líquidos en ambientes de microgravedad, medir la efectividad de varios extintores de incendios gaseosos como CO2, He y SF6, y desarrollar modelos predictivos confiables para los límites de combustión en condiciones de gravedad reducida. La misión busca validar y mejorar modelos simplificados incorporando reacciones químicas detalladas, transferencia de calor y movimiento de materiales, utilizando tanto datos espaciales como pruebas exhaustivas en tierra. Los impactos de la investigación y los beneficios para la Tierra de la misión FLEX son significativos y multifacéticos.
key_findings: FLEX mapped the limiting oxygen index of liquid fuels in microgravity as a function of pressure from 0.5 to 1.5 atm and tested CO2, helium, and SF6 as gaseous suppressants.
It measured droplet burning rates, extinction behavior, soot levels, heat radiation, and temperature profiles for free and fiber-supported droplets, including slow sub-buoyant drift.
The campaign provides a microgravity database for fire-suppression effectiveness and for validating droplet-combustion and flammability models.
key_findings_es: FLEX mapeó el índice límite de oxígeno de combustibles líquidos en microgravedad en función de la presión de 0,5 a 1,5 atm y evaluó CO2, helio y SF6 como extintores gaseosos.

Midió velocidades de combustión de gotas, comportamiento de extinción, niveles de hollín, radiación térmica y perfiles de temperatura en gotas libres y soportadas por fibra, incluida una deriva lenta subflotante.
La campaña aporta una base de datos en microgravedad para la eficacia de la supresión de incendios y para validar modelos de combustión de gotas e inflamabilidad.
limitations: The iterative LOI procedure could not resolve extinction droplets that were too small for the available diagnostics, introducing uncertainty in some limits.
Single-droplet suppressant tests do not directly scale to compartment fires, and the public metadata omits the LOI tables.
limitations_es: El procedimiento iterativo del LOI no pudo resolver gotas en extinción demasiado pequeñas para los diagnósticos disponibles, lo que introduce incertidumbre en algunos límites.
Los ensayos de extintores con gotas individuales no escalan directamente a incendios de compartimento, y los metadatos públicos omiten las tablas de LOI.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
investigations.title_es: Experimento de extinción de llamas - 2
investigations.objective:
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
investigations.approach:
The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.

The overall investigation approach can be summarized as:
 1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity.
 2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures.
 3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter.
 4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment.
 5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion.
 6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.
 7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed.
 8. Analyze data.

The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.
investigations.research_impacts:
The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to:

 1) More sustainable energy production.
 2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
 3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
 4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

investigations.summary_en:
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
 1. The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector.
investigations.summary_es:
El objetivo principal de los experimentos de vuelo de FLEX-2 es extender los resultados de FLEX-1 a combustibles y condiciones ambientales que imiten las condiciones reales de la cámara de combustión, así como proporcionar datos experimentales de referencia sobre la combustión de gotas de dos componentes en una amplia gama de condiciones iniciales para validar simulaciones numéricas y desarrollar nuevos modelos teóricos. Los objetivos experimentales detallados se pueden detallar además como:
 1. La combustión de combustibles líquidos es la abrumadora fuente de energía en el sector del transporte.
key_findings: FLEX-2 burned bi-component and pure fuel droplets in microgravity at pressures from 0.5 to 3.0 atm and oxygen mole fractions from 0.1 to 0.4, including binary droplet arrays.
The experiments examined liquid-phase mixing, soot-shell dynamics, flame extinction boundaries, and droplet interactions, with high-speed imaging and chamber diagnostics.
The dataset provides benchmark validation for droplet-combustion models and supports the development of fuel surrogates for practical combustors.
key_findings_es: FLEX-2 quemó gotas de combustible puras y bicomponentes en microgravedad a presiones de 0,5 a 3,0 atm y fracciones molares de oxígeno de 0,1 a 0,4, incluidos arreglos binarios de gotas.

Los experimentos examinaron la mezcla en fase líquida, la dinámica de la capa de hollín, los límites de extinción y las interacciones entre gotas, con imágenes de alta velocidad y diagnóstico de cámara.
El conjunto de datos aporta validación de referencia para modelos de combustión de gotas y respalda el desarrollo de sustitutos de combustible para combustores prácticos.
limitations: Droplet sizes, support fibers, and array configurations are necessarily limited, and the results do not reproduce the full spray environment of an engine.
The public record contains objectives and impacts but not the measured burning-rate or extinction data.
limitations_es: Los tamaños de gota, las fibras de soporte y las configuraciones de arreglos son necesariamente limitados, y los resultados no reproducen el entorno completo de pulverización de un motor.
El registro público contiene objetivos e impactos, pero no los datos medidos de velocidad de combustión ni de extinción.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
investigations.title_es: Prueba de viabilidad de medición de polvo y aerosoles/Prueba de viabilidad de medición de polvo y aerosoles-2
investigations.objective:
The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
investigations.approach:
The experimental approach consists of the following components:

 1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
 2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
 3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
investigations.research_impacts: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

investigations.summary_es: El objetivo de DAFT/DAFT-2 fue mitigar el riesgo del Experimento de medición de aerosoles de humo (SAME). SAME se basó en un contador de núcleos de condensado disponible comercialmente, el TSI P-Trak, para cuantificar aerosoles de humo en un entorno de microgravedad; sin embargo, existía la preocupación de que el P-Trak no fuera confiable en microgravedad, ya que depende de la gravedad para reciclar el alcohol isopropílico utilizado en el proceso de medición. Las misiones de vuelos espaciales de duración prolongada con naves más grandes requerirán sistemas de detección de incendios con mayor confiabilidad y sensibilidad.
key_findings: DAFT/DAFT-2 redesigned the TSI P-Trak for microgravity by replacing gravity-driven alcohol recycling with capillary forces and removing the orientation mercury switch.
The modified counter was tested on orbit against the DustTrak using Arizona Red Dust aerosol standards in 15-liter Mylar bags.
The campaign demonstrated that the modified P-Trak can operate in microgravity and reduced the technical risk for the SAME smoke-aerosol experiment.
key_findings_es: DAFT/DAFT-2 rediseñó el TSI P-Trak para microgravedad reemplazando el reciclaje de alcohol por gravedad con fuerzas capilares y eliminando el interruptor de mercurio de orientación.
El contador modificado se probó en órbita frente al DustTrak usando estándares de aerosol de polvo rojo de Arizona en bolsas Mylar de 15 litros.
La campaña demostró que el P-Trak modificado puede operar en microgravedad y redujo el riesgo técnico del experimento de aerosoles de humo SAME.
limitations: Arizona Red Dust is a surrogate aerosol, not combustion smoke, so the test validates instrument function rather than smoke-detection performance.
The public metadata does not report the counting agreement between the two instruments; that result is in the project documentation.
limitations_es: El polvo rojo de Arizona es un aerosol sustituto, no humo de combustión, por lo que el ensayo valida el funcionamiento del instrumento y no el desempeño de detección de humo.

investigations.title: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.title_es: Investigación de llamas frías
investigations.sponsoring_agency: ISSNL National Laboratory - National Science Foundation (NL-NSF)
investigations.objective:
The objectives of this investigation are to:
 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
investigations.approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.
investigations.research_impacts:
A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

investigations.summary_es:
Los objetivos de esta investigación son:
 1) Examinar el comportamiento de combustión del n-dodecano y de las mezclas de n-dodecano/isododecano a presiones que oscilan entre 0,25 atm y 5 atm. 2) Analizar los efectos de la dilución con helio sobre el comportamiento de la llama fría. Una comprensión básica de las llamas frías es importante para comprender los fenómenos de ignición de combustibles prácticos y aditivos para combustibles.
key_findings: CFI burned n-dodecane, farnesane, and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets in the CIR/MDCA facility at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm, with helium dilution and controlled oxygen atmospheres.
The experiments examined droplet size, pressure, flame extinction, soot formation, and low-temperature cool-flame behavior using droplet imaging, OH* imaging, and radiometry.
The results support kinetic-mechanism validation and the design of cleaner HCCI and diesel combustion, where cool-flame reactivity affects octane and cetane behavior.
key_findings_es: CFI quemó gotas de n-dodecano, farnesano y mezclas n-dodecano/iso-dodecano en la instalación CIR/MDCA a presiones de 0,25 a 5 atm, con dilución de helio y atmósferas de oxígeno controladas.

Los experimentos examinaron tamaño de gota, presión, extinción de llama, formación de hollín y comportamiento de llama fría de baja temperatura mediante imágenes de gotas, imágenes de OH* y radiometría.
Los resultados respaldan la validación de mecanismos cinéticos y el diseño de combustión HCCI y diésel más limpia, donde la reactividad de llama fría afecta el octanaje y el número de cetano.
limitations: Droplet combustion is a small-scale, idealized configuration; soot and extinction behavior may differ in sprays and full-scale combustors.
The public record does not include the measured extinction diameters or soot data, and the pressure range stops at 5 atm.
limitations_es: La combustión de gotas es una configuración idealizada y de pequeña escala; el hollín y la extinción pueden diferir en pulverizaciones y combustores de escala real.
El registro público no incluye los diámetros de extinción ni los datos de hollín medidos, y el rango de presión termina en 5 atm.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
investigations.title_es: Combustión avanzada mediante experimentos de microgravedad: estructura y respuesta de llamas de difusión esféricas
investigations.objective:
A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):
 Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
 Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
 Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.
investigations.approach:
A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames.
Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.
investigations.research_impacts: The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

key_findings: s-Flame established spherical diffusion flames on a porous burner with hydrogen/methane/ethylene fuels and nitrogen, helium, or CO2 dilution, and measured their transient temperature and species structure.

The data provide a one-dimensional benchmark for transport properties, detailed kinetics, chemiluminescence, and radiative heat loss in buoyancy-free diffusion flames.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.title_es: Experimentos de combustión avanzada mediante microgravedad Efectos del campo eléctrico en llamas de difusión laminar
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
investigations.approach:
The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.
All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.
investigations.research_impacts: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
investigations.title_es: Combustión avanzada mediante experimentos de microgravedad / Llama de difusión laminar de coflujo
investigations.objective:
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.
investigations.approach: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.
investigations.research_impacts: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.title_es: Combustión avanzada mediante experimentos de microgravedad: emulador de velocidad de combustión
investigations.objective:
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
investigations.approach:
To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests.

For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared.

The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions.

In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions.

We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.
investigations.research_impacts: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

investigations.sponsoring_agency: National Science Foundation (NSF) Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS)
investigations.objective:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
investigations.approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
investigations.research_impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

key_findings: CFI-G conducted spherical diffusion-flame tests on the ISS with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane, in normal and inverse convection and over a broad range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic temperature, and flow rate.
The campaign was paired with CFD simulations to identify a chemical-kinetics mechanism that reproduces the measured cool diffusion flames, whose peak temperatures lie between roughly 500 and 1000 K.
The results target ultra-lean combustion and higher-efficiency engines by improving the low-temperature chemistry needed to predict cool-flame onset and stability.
key_findings_es: CFI-G realizó ensayos de llamas de difusión esféricas en la ISS con propano, n-butano y n-pentano, en convección normal e inversa y en un amplio rango de fracción de mezcla estequiométrica, temperatura adiabática y caudal.

La campaña se combinó con simulaciones CFD para identificar un mecanismo de cinética química que reproduzca las llamas frías de difusión medidas, cuyas temperaturas máximas se sitúan aproximadamente entre 500 y 1000 K.
Los resultados apuntan a la combustión ultra-pobre y a motores más eficientes al mejorar la química de baja temperatura necesaria para predecir el inicio y la estabilidad de las llamas frías.
limitations: Cool diffusion flames are a gaseous, laboratory-scale phenomenon; the results inform but do not directly certify spacecraft material flammability.
The public record does not report the final measured cool-flame limits or the validated mechanism; those require the project publications.
limitations_es: Las llamas frías de difusión son un fenómeno gaseoso y de laboratorio; los resultados informan, pero no certifican directamente la inflamabilidad de materiales de nave.
El registro público no reporta los límites finales medidos de llama fría ni el mecanismo validado; estos requieren las publicaciones del proyecto.

investigations.title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
investigations.title_es: Estudios cuantitativos de transiciones de llama fría en extinción por radiación/estiramiento utilizando llamas de contraflujo
investigations.objective:
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.
investigations.approach:
Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].
investigations.research_impacts: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

investigations.summary_es:
Al utilizar los datos experimentales de extinción de llamas (FLEX) del sistema de ciencias de la combustión de Ciencias Físicas e Informática (PSI), el propósito de esta subvención fue realizar nuevas simulaciones y experimentos terrestres utilizando llamas de contraflujo sensibilizadas con ozono para:
 1) Desarrollar un nuevo diagrama de los límites de inflamabilidad de llamas frías por difusión afectadas por radiación, difusión y convección. 2) Cerrar la brecha de conocimiento entre los límites de inflamabilidad y los límites de extinción de llamas calientes y llamas frías. Obtener una comprensión fundamental de la llama de difusión cálida es particularmente relevante para la combustión en campos de flujo altamente turbulentos y en entornos de microgravedad, debido a la posibilidad de largos tiempos de residencia.
key_findings: The investigation combined FLEX data with ozone-sensitized counterflow simulations and ground experiments to build a flammability-limit diagram for cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
It identified a double reaction zone in warm flames and showed that the flammable region of cool and warm flames expands with pressure, up to the 20 atm cases studied.
The results bridge cool-flame and hot-flame extinction limits and provide quantitative targets for kinetic and radiation model validation.
key_findings_es: La investigación combinó datos de FLEX con simulaciones y experimentos en tierra de llamas contracorriente sensibilizadas con ozono para construir un diagrama de límites de inflamabilidad de llamas frías afectadas por radiación, difusión y convección.
Identificó una doble zona de reacción en llamas tibias y mostró que la región inflamable de llamas frías y tibias se amplía con la presión, hasta los casos de 20 atm estudiados.
Los resultados conectan los límites de extinción de llamas frías y calientes y aportan objetivos cuantitativos para validar modelos cinéticos y de radiación.
limitations: Ozone sensitization and one-dimensional counterflow geometry are controlled idealizations; direct transfer to microgravity droplet or spacecraft fires needs additional study.
The public metadata summarizes the findings without the full extinction-limit tables, which are distributed across the cited publications.
limitations_es: La sensibilización con ozono y la geometría contracorriente unidimensional son idealizaciones controladas; su traslado directo a gotas en microgravedad o incendios en naves requiere estudios adicionales.
Los metadatos públicos resumen los hallazgos sin las tablas completas de límites de extinción, que se distribuyen en las publicaciones citadas.

investigations.title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.title_es: Experimento de punto de humo en coflujo
investigations.objective:
The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
investigations.approach: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.
investigations.research_impacts:
(1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments.
(2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions.
(3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation
(4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

investigations.summary_es:
El objetivo de SPICE es comprender mejor el complejo proceso de combustión mediante la observación de llamas en un entorno de microgravedad a bordo de la Estación Espacial Internacional (ISS) y experimentos terrestres análogos. Los objetivos específicos fueron:
(1) Identificar las propiedades del punto de humo laminar de llamas de difusión en chorro no flotantes en diversas condiciones de coflujo en microgravedad. (1) Mejorará nuestra comprensión de los mecanismos de formación de hollín y ayudará a diseñar entornos de naves espaciales más seguros.
key_findings: SPICE studied 526 non-buoyant jet diffusion flames across three burner diameters (0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm) and coflow velocities from 5.4 to 65 cm/s.
It identified smoke-point properties and luminous flame lengths for methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures, linking soot propensity to fuel and flow conditions.
The dataset supports correlations between luminous flame shape and residence time and provides validation data for soot-formation models under microgravity.
key_findings_es: SPICE estudió 526 llamas de difusión tipo chorro sin flotabilidad con tres diámetros de quemador (0,41, 0,76 y 1,6 mm) y velocidades de coflujo de 5,4 a 65 cm/s.

Identificó las propiedades del punto de humo y las longitudes de llama luminosa para metano, etileno, propano, propileno y mezclas de propileno, relacionando la propensión al hollín con el combustible y el flujo.
El conjunto de datos respalda correlaciones entre la forma de la llama luminosa y el tiempo de residencia, y aporta datos de validación para modelos de formación de hollín en microgravedad.
limitations: The smoke point is an optical threshold and does not by itself resolve the full soot volume fraction or aggregate structure.
Only gaseous fuels were tested, and the public metadata does not include the 526-flame data table.
limitations_es: El punto de humo es un umbral óptico y por sí solo no resuelve la fracción volumétrica de hollín ni la estructura de los agregados.

investigations.title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.title_es: Experimento de estructura y despegue en combustión.
investigations.objective:
Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
investigations.approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.
investigations.research_impacts:
1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.
2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.
3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety.
4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.

investigations.title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.title_es: Experimento de medición de humo y aerosoles
investigations.objective: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
investigations.approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
investigations.research_impacts: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material,
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. investigations.objective:
The primary objectives of this flight experiment are:
A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames.
B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames.
C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.
investigations.approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
investigations.research_impacts: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

investigations.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
investigations.title_es: Modelado simultáneo de propagación de llamas utilizando colectores generados por Flamelet en microgravedad en comparación con experimentos BASS utilizando tomografía de dos colores
investigations.objective:
The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
investigations.approach:
The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.
Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.
investigations.research_impacts: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.
